lessons.title: Laws of indices and their applications
objectives: State and apply the laws of indices.
Evaluate expressions with zero, negative and fractional indices.
Simplify algebraic expressions involving indices.
lessons.body:
In aᵐ, a is the base and m is the index (power or exponent): aᵐ means a multiplied by itself m times.

LAWS (a and b are non-zero real numbers; m and n are rational numbers):
1. aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (multiplication law)
2. aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (division law)
3. (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ (power of a power)
4. (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ and (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ
5. a⁰ = 1
6. a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
7. a^(p/q) = (q-th root of a)ᵖ, i.e. a^(1/2) = √a, a^(1/3) = ∛a, a^(2/3) = (∛a)².

Example 1. p³ × p² = (p × p × p) × (p × p) = p⁵. Also 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128.
Example 2. (3²)³ = 3⁶ = 729.
Example 3. 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4. 25^(3/2) = (√25)³ = 125.
Example 4. 27^(–2/3) = 1/27^(2/3) = 1/(∛27)² = 1/9.
Example 5. (1/4)^(–1/2) = 4^(1/2) = 2 (a negative index inverts the base).
Example 6. Simplify (x³y²)² ÷ (x²y) = x⁶y⁴ ÷ x²y = x⁴y³.
Example 7. (0.000001)² : 0.000001 = 10⁻⁶, so the value is 10⁻¹² = 0.000000000001.

Always reduce to a single base and a single power before evaluating, and check the sign of each index.

practice.prompt: Evaluate 64^(2/3).
Evaluate 16^(–3/4).
Simplify 2⁵ × 2⁻³ ÷ 2⁰.
Simplify (2a²b)³ ÷ (4ab²).
practice.marking: 1 mark expansion, 1 mark each of coefficient and indices.

lessons.title: Indicial and exponential equations, including quadratic form
objectives: Solve exponential equations by equating powers of the same base.
Solve exponential equations of quadratic form by substitution.
lessons.body:
RULE. If the bases are equal (and not 0, 1 or –1), the powers are equal: aˣ = aʸ ⇔ x = y. So the first step is to write both sides with the SAME base.

LINEAR FORM
Example 1. (1/2)ˣ = 8. Write 1/2 = 2⁻¹ and 8 = 2³: 2⁻ˣ = 2³, so –x = 3 and x = –3.
Example 2. (0.25)ˣ⁺¹ = 16. 0.25 = 4⁻¹ and 16 = 4²: 4⁻⁽ˣ⁺¹⁾ = 4², so –(x + 1) = 2 and x = –3.
Example 3. 3ˣ = 1/81 = 3⁻⁴, so x = –4.
Example 4. 10ˣ = 1/0.001 = 1000 = 10³, so x = 3.
Example 5. 4/2ˣ = 64ˣ. 4/2ˣ = 2²⁻ˣ and 64ˣ = 2⁶ˣ, so 2 – x = 6x and x = 2/7.

QUADRATIC FORM. Substitute y = aˣ and solve the quadratic in y; then reject any y ≤ 0 (aˣ is always positive).
Example 6. 2²ˣ – 6(2ˣ) + 8 = 0. Let y = 2ˣ: y² – 6y + 8 = 0, (y – 2)(y – 4) = 0, y = 2 or 4. So 2ˣ = 2 gives x = 1 and 2ˣ = 4 gives x = 2.
Example 7. 2²ˣ⁺¹ – 5(2ˣ) + 2 = 0. Write 2²ˣ⁺¹ = 2 × (2ˣ)²: 2y² – 5y + 2 = 0, (2y – 1)(y – 2) = 0, y = 1/2 or 2. So x = –1 or x = 1.
Example 8. 3²ˣ – 4(3ˣ⁺¹) + 27 = 0. 3ˣ⁺¹ = 3 × 3ˣ so y² – 12y + 27 = 0, (y – 3)(y – 9) = 0, y = 3 or 9: x = 1 or x = 2.
Example 9. 3²ˣ – 9 = 0 gives 3²ˣ = 3², x = 1.

Check each answer by substituting it back.

practice.prompt: Solve 2ˣ = 0.125.
Solve 3⁻ˣ = 243.
Solve 25ˣ = 625.

practice.answer: y² – 10y + 16 = 0, y = 2 or 8, so x = 1 or x = 3.
practice.marking: 1 mark substitution, 1 mark factors, 1 mark each x.

practice.answer: y = 3ˣ: y² – 4y + 3 = 0, y = 1 or 3, so x = 0 or x = 1.
practice.marking: 1 mark substitution, 1 mark y, 1 mark each x.

lessons.title: Logarithms: laws, equations and change of base
objectives: Convert between index and logarithmic form.
Apply the laws of logarithms to simplify and solve.
Use change of base and standard form (characteristic and mantissa) with tables.
lessons.body:
DEFINITION. aˣ = N ⇔ logₐ N = x (a > 0, a ≠ 1, N > 0). Logarithm to base 10 is written lg or log.
Examples: 2⁵ = 32 ⇔ log₂ 32 = 5; 3⁻² = 1/9 ⇔ log₃(1/9) = –2; log₁₀ 0.001 = –3.

LAWS
1. log(MN) = log M + log N
2. log(M/N) = log M – log N
3. log Mᵖ = p log M
4. logₐ a = 1 and logₐ 1 = 0
5. CHANGE OF BASE: log_a b = log_c b ÷ log_c a (so log_a b = 1/log_b a).

Example 1. log 2 + log 5 = log 10 = 1.
Example 2. Write log 12 in terms of log 2 and log 3: log 12 = log(2² × 3) = 2 log 2 + log 3.
Example 3. Solve log₂(x + 3) + log₂(x – 3) = 4. Then (x + 3)(x – 3) = 2⁴ = 16, x² = 25, x = 5 or –5. For x = –5 the logarithm of a negative number does not exist, so x = 5.
Example 4. Solve log₁₀(4x² + 1) – 2 log₁₀ x – log₁₀ 2 = 1. Combine: log[(4x² + 1)/(2x²)] = 1, so (4x² + 1)/(2x²) = 10, 4x² + 1 = 20x², x² = 1/16, x = 1/4 (x > 0). Check: (4/16 + 1)/(2/16) = 1.25/0.125 = 10 ✓.
Example 5. log₂ 3 = log 3 ÷ log 2 = 0.4771 ÷ 0.3010 = 1.585.

STANDARD FORM AND TABLES. A number N = A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10. log N = n + log A: n is the characteristic and log A (from tables, between 0 and 1) is the mantissa. log 3450 = 3.5378; log 0.00345 = –3 + 0.5378, written 3̄.5378 (bar 3 means –3 + 0.5378 = –2.4622).
Multiplication: 24.5 × 3.2 : log 24.5 = 1.3892, log 3.2 = 0.5051, sum = 1.8943, antilog gives 78.4.

practice.prompt: Write 5³ = 125 in logarithmic form and evaluate log₃ 81.
Express log(a²b/c) in terms of log a, log b and log c.
practice.answer: 2 log a + log b – log c.

practice.prompt: Solve log₃ x + log₃(x – 2) = 1.
practice.answer: x(x – 2) = 3, x² – 2x – 3 = 0, x = 3 or –1; reject –1, so x = 3.
practice.marking: 1 mark combine, 1 mark equation, 1 mark rejection.

practice.prompt: Find x if 2ˣ = 7, using logarithms (3 d.p.).
Using tables, log 5.6 = 0.7482. Write down log 560 and log 0.056.

lessons.title: Sequences and series: the arithmetic progression
objectives: Define a sequence and an arithmetic progression (AP).
Use Tₙ = a + (n – 1)d and Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n – 1)d].
Find arithmetic means.
lessons.body:
A SEQUENCE is a list of numbers in a definite order (terms T₁, T₂, T₃, …). A SERIES is the sum of the terms.

An ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION (AP) has a constant common difference d = T₂ – T₁ = T₃ – T₂ = …
nth term: Tₙ = a + (n – 1)d, where a is the first term.
Sum of the first n terms: Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n – 1)d] = (n/2)(a + l), where l is the last term.
Arithmetic mean of two numbers a and b: (a + b)/2. To insert k arithmetic means between a and b, the common difference is d = (b – a)/(k + 1).

Example 1. 3, 7, 11, … a = 3, d = 4. T₁₀ = 3 + 9(4) = 39. S₁₀ = 5(6 + 36) = 210.
Example 2. How many terms are in 5, 8, 11, …, 62? 5 + (n – 1)3 = 62, n – 1 = 19, n = 20.
Example 3. Insert 3 arithmetic means between 4 and 20: d = 16/4 = 4, so 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.
Example 4. The 3rd term of an AP is 11 and the 7th is 27. T₇ – T₃ = 4d = 16, d = 4, a = 11 – 8 = 3.
Example 5. Sum of the first 20 positive even numbers: a = 2, d = 2, S₂₀ = 10(4 + 38) = 420.
Why Sₙ works: write the sum forwards and backwards and add; every pair totals (a + l) and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n(a + l).

practice.prompt: Find the sum of the integers from 1 to 100.
The 4th term of an AP is 14 and the 9th is 34. Find a and d.

lessons.title: Geometric progressions: nth term, sums, geometric mean and sum to infinity
objectives: Use Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹ and the sum formulas of a GP.
Find a geometric mean.
Find the sum to infinity when |r| < 1.
lessons.body:
A GEOMETRIC PROGRESSION (GP) multiplies each term by a constant common ratio r = T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₂ = …
nth term: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = a(rⁿ – 1)/(r – 1) (use when r > 1) or Sₙ = a(1 – rⁿ)/(1 – r) (use when r < 1).
Sum to infinity (only if |r| < 1): S∞ = a/(1 – r).
Geometric mean of positive numbers a and b: √(ab).

Example 1. 2, 6, 18, … a = 2, r = 3. T₆ = 2(3⁵) = 486. S₆ = 2(3⁶ – 1)/2 = 728.
Example 2. 8, 4, 2, … a = 8, r = 1/2. S∞ = 8/(1 – 1/2) = 16.
Example 3. The geometric mean of 4 and 25 is √100 = 10 (so 4, 10, 25 is a GP with r = 2.5).
Example 4. Which term of 3, 6, 12, … is 192? 3(2ⁿ⁻¹) = 192, 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 64 = 2⁶, n = 7.
Example 5. Write 0.333… as a fraction: 0.3 + 0.03 + 0.003 + … is a GP with a = 0.3, r = 0.1, so S∞ = 0.3/0.9 = 1/3.
Example 6. T₂ = 6 and T₅ = 48: r³ = 48/6 = 8, r = 2, a = 3.

practice.marking: 1 mark each of a, r, answer.

lessons.title: Linear and quadratic inequalities in one variable, and absolute values
objectives: Solve linear inequalities and show solutions on a number line.
Solve quadratic inequalities.
Solve inequalities involving absolute value.
lessons.body:
RULES. You may add or subtract the same number on both sides, and multiply or divide by a POSITIVE number, without changing the sign. Multiplying or dividing by a NEGATIVE number reverses the inequality sign.

LINEAR. Example 1. 3x – 5 < 7 gives 3x < 12 and x < 4. Example 2. –2x ≥ 8 gives x ≤ –4 (sign reversed). Example 3. 2 < 3x – 1 ≤ 11 gives 3 < 3x ≤ 12, so 1 < x ≤ 4.

QUADRATIC. Factorise, find the critical values, then test the intervals between them.
Example 4. x² – 5x + 6 < 0: (x – 2)(x – 3) < 0. The product is negative between the roots: 2 < x < 3.
Example 5. x² – x – 6 ≥ 0: (x – 3)(x + 2) ≥ 0. The product is non-negative outside the roots: x ≤ –2 or x ≥ 3.
(For a parabola opening upwards, y < 0 between the roots and y > 0 outside them.)

ABSOLUTE VALUE. |x| is the distance of x from 0. |x| < a means –a < x < a; |x| > a means x < –a or x > a.
Example 6. |x – 3| < 5 gives –5 < x – 3 < 5, so –2 < x < 8.
Example 7. |2x + 1| ≥ 7 gives 2x + 1 ≥ 7 or 2x + 1 ≤ –7, so x ≥ 3 or x ≤ –4.

On a number line a filled dot means the end value is included (≤ or ≥) and an open dot means it is not (< or >).

practice.prompt: Solve 5 – 2x > 1.
Solve x² + 2x – 8 ≤ 0.
Solve |x + 2| ≤ 3.
Solve x² > 9.
Solve –3 < 2x + 1 < 9.

lessons.title: Inequalities in two variables, graphical solution and linear programming
objectives: Show a linear inequality in two variables as a region.
Find the region satisfying several inequalities.
Maximise or minimise an objective function at the vertices.
lessons.body:
A LINEAR INEQUALITY IN TWO VARIABLES, e.g. x + y ≤ 6, is shown as a region of the plane.
1. Draw the boundary line x + y = 6 (find two points, e.g. (0, 6) and (6, 0)).
2. Use a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >.
3. Test a point not on the line (usually the origin): 0 + 0 ≤ 6 is true, so the side containing (0, 0) is the required side.
4. For several inequalities, the solution is the region satisfying ALL of them. State whether you shade the wanted or the unwanted region and label it.

LINEAR PROGRAMMING finds the largest or smallest value of an objective function such as P = ax + by over a feasible region. The optimum occurs at a vertex (corner) of the region, so list the vertices and evaluate P at each.
Example. Maximise P = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Vertices: (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1), (0, 4). P = 0, 9, 11, 8. The maximum is 11 at (3, 1).
(For a word problem define x and y first, write each condition as an inequality, draw the region, then test the vertices.)

lessons.title: Functions: one-to-one and onto mappings, composite and inverse functions
objectives: Define one-to-one and onto mappings.
Form composite functions fg(x) and gf(x).
Find the inverse f⁻¹(x) of a function.
lessons.body:
A mapping f : X → Y gives each element of X exactly one image in Y. It is ONE-TO-ONE if different elements have different images, and ONTO if every element of Y is the image of some element of X (the range equals the co-domain).

COMPOSITE FUNCTION. fg(x) = f(g(x)): apply g first, then f. In general fg ≠ gf.
Example 1. f(x) = 3x – 1 and g(x) = x². fg(x) = 3x² – 1; gf(x) = (3x – 1)².
Example 2. f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = 2x. fg(x) = 2x + 4; gf(x) = 2(x + 4) = 2x + 8.

INVERSE FUNCTION. f⁻¹ undoes f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Method: write y = f(x), swap the roles of x and y (make x the subject), then replace y by x.
Example 3. f(x) = 2x + 3: y = 2x + 3, x = (y – 3)/2, so f⁻¹(x) = (x – 3)/2.
Example 4. f(x) = (x + 1)/(x – 2), x ≠ 2. y(x – 2) = x + 1, xy – 2y = x + 1, x(y – 1) = 2y + 1, so f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 1)/(x – 1), x ≠ 1. Check: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.
Only a one-to-one function has an inverse function. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

lessons.title: Trigonometric ratios, special angles, general angles and identities
objectives: Define the six trigonometric ratios.
Use the exact values for 30°, 45° and 60°.
Use quadrant rules and the basic identities.
lessons.body:
RATIOS. In a right-angled triangle, for an acute angle θ: sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj = sin θ/cos θ. Reciprocals: sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.

SPECIAL ANGLES (from an equilateral triangle of side 2 and an isosceles right triangle):
sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3.

IDENTITIES: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

GENERAL ANGLES. Measure the angle anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. In quadrant 1 all ratios are positive; in quadrant 2 only sine; in quadrant 3 only tangent; in quadrant 4 only cosine ("All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine"). Reduce to an acute angle: sin(180° – θ) = sin θ, cos(180° – θ) = –cos θ, tan(180° – θ) = –tan θ; sin(180° + θ) = –sin θ, cos(180° + θ) = –cos θ, tan(180° + θ) = tan θ; sin(360° – θ) = –sin θ, cos(360° – θ) = cos θ, tan(360° – θ) = –tan θ.

Example 1. sin θ = 5/13, θ acute: cos θ = 12/13, tan θ = 5/12, sec θ = 13/12.
Example 2. sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2; cos 210° = –cos 30° = –√3/2; tan 300° = –tan 60° = –√3.
Example 3. Show (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ: expand to sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ and use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
Example 4. Solve sin θ = 1/2 for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°: θ = 30° or 150°.

Simplify cos θ tan θ.
practice.answer: cos θ × (sin θ/cos θ) = sin θ.

lessons.title: Flowcharts: symbols, algorithms and tracing
objectives: Name the standard flowchart symbols.
Draw and trace a flowchart for a simple problem.
lessons.body:
A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of a solution (an algorithm) in order. Standard symbols: an OVAL for Start and Stop; a PARALLELOGRAM for input or output; a RECTANGLE for a process (a calculation); a DIAMOND for a decision with two exits labelled Yes and No; ARROWS for the direction of flow.

Advantages: it helps in planning a computer program; it makes a solution easy to follow and to check; it exposes errors in the logic before coding.

Example 1 (perimeter of a rectangle). Start → Input l and b → P = 2(l + b) → Output P → Stop. For l = 7 and b = 3, P = 20.
Example 2 (even or odd). Start → Input n → Is n ÷ 2 a whole number? Yes → Output "even"; No → Output "odd" → Stop.
Example 3 (tracing a loop). Set S = 0 and i = 1. Decision: is i ≤ 4? If Yes: S = S + i, i = i + 1, go back to the decision; if No: output S. Trace: i = 1, S = 1; i = 2, S = 3; i = 3, S = 6; i = 4, S = 10; i = 5 stops, output 10.
Use a trace table (columns for each variable) to check a flowchart with test values.

practice.prompt: Draw (describe step by step) a flowchart for the area of a triangle, ½ × base × height.
practice.answer: Start; Input b and h; A = ½ × b × h; Output A; Stop.
practice.marking: 1 mark symbols, 1 mark order, 1 mark formula.

practice.prompt: Trace Example 3 with 'is i ≤ 5?' instead and state the output.
Describe a flowchart that outputs the larger of two numbers a and b.
practice.answer: Input a, b; Is a > b? Yes: Output a; No: Output b; Stop.

practice.prompt: State two advantages of using a flowchart.
practice.answer: Any two: easier to understand, aids planning of a program, helps find errors.

lessons.title: Gradients of straight lines and curves
objectives: Calculate the gradient of a line from two points or from its equation.
Use y = mx + c, and the rules for parallel and perpendicular lines.
Estimate the gradient of a curve at a point.
lessons.body:
The gradient (slope) of a line measures how steeply y changes with x: m = (y₂ – y₁)/(x₂ – x₁).

Example 1. P(7, –2) and Q(–1, 2): m = (2 – (–2))/(–1 – 7) = 4/(–8) = –1/2.
Example 2. Gradient of 7x + 4y – 8 = 0: 4y = –7x + 8, y = –(7/4)x + 2, so m = –7/4 and the y-intercept is 2.
Example 3. Sketch 4x – 3y = 12: x = 0 gives y = –4 (point (0, –4)); y = 0 gives x = 3 (point (3, 0)). m = 4/3.
Lines parallel to the x-axis have the form y = c (gradient 0). Lines parallel to the y-axis have the form x = a (gradient undefined).
Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines satisfy m₁m₂ = –1.

GRADIENT OF A CURVE. The gradient at a point of a curve is the gradient of the tangent at that point.
Example 4. y = x²/4 for x = –2 to 3: y = 1, 0.25, 0, 0.25, 1, 2.25 (x = –2, –1, 0, 1, 2, 3). Draw the curve and the tangent at x = 3: it rises about 1.5 for each 1 across, so the gradient is 1.5. At x = –2 the tangent falls 1 for each 1 across, so the gradient is –1. A check by chords: from (3, 2.25) to (3.5, 3.0625) the gradient is 1.625, close to 1.5; shorter chords get closer.

lessons.title: Angle of slope and the angle between two lines
objectives: Find the angle of slope of a line from its gradient.
Find the angle between two lines.
lessons.body:
The ANGLE OF SLOPE θ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise, and tan θ = m (the gradient).
Example 1. Line through (3, 2) and (7, 10): m = 8/4 = 2, so θ = tan⁻¹ 2 = 63.4°.
If m is negative, θ is obtuse: θ = 180° – tan⁻¹|m|. For m = –1, θ = 135°. For m = –√3, θ = 120°.

ANGLE BETWEEN TWO LINES with gradients m₁ and m₂: tan φ = |(m₁ – m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
Example 2. m₁ = 2 and m₂ = 1/3: tan φ = (2 – 1/3)/(1 + 2/3) = (5/3)/(5/3) = 1, so φ = 45°. (Alternatively θ₁ = 63.4°, θ₂ = 18.4°, and 63.4° – 18.4° = 45°.)
If m₁m₂ = –1 the denominator is 0 and the lines are perpendicular (φ = 90°). If m₁ = m₂ the numerator is 0 and the lines are parallel.

lessons.title: Vectors: modulus, unit vectors, direction cosines and arithmetic
objectives: Find the modulus of a vector.
Find a unit vector and direction cosines.
Add, subtract and scale vectors in component form.
lessons.body:
A vector r = ai + bj (or ai + bj + ck) has MODULUS |r| = √(a² + b²) (or √(a² + b² + c²)). The zero vector has modulus 0; the negative vector –a has the same size and opposite direction; two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction.
Example 1. |3i + 4j| = √(9 + 16) = 5; |–2i – 5j| = √29; |3i – 4j + 12k| = √(9 + 16 + 144) = 13.

UNIT VECTOR in the direction of r: r̂ = r/|r|, and |r̂| = 1.
Example 2. r = 2i + 3j: |r| = √13, r̂ = (2i + 3j)/√13. q = 4i – 5j: |q| = √41, q̂ = (4i – 5j)/√41. p = 7i + 2j – 3k: |p| = √62, p̂ = (7i + 2j – 3k)/√62.

DIRECTION COSINES of r = ai + bj + ck are a/|r|, b/|r|, c/|r| (the cosines of the angles r makes with the axes); their squares add to 1.
Example 3. r = 2i + 3j + 6k: |r| = 7; direction cosines 2/7, 3/7, 6/7.

ARITHMETIC: add and subtract component by component; multiply every component by a scalar.
Example 4. p = 2i – 3j, q = 3i + 5j, r = i + j. 2p + q + 3r = (4i – 6j) + (3i + 5j) + (3i + 3j) = 10i + 2j. 3p – 2q = (6i – 9j) – (6i + 10j) = –19j.
Example 5. AB = a – b and AC = 2a + 3b, with a = 2i + 3j and b = 3i – 2j. BC = AC – AB = a + 4b = (2i + 3j) + (12i – 8j) = 14i – 5j.

NOTE: the source note's Example (3p – 2q) uses 3p = 9i – 9j, which does not follow from p = 2i – 3j; the corrected working above is used here.

lessons.title: The equation of a straight line: gradient–point and two-point forms
objectives: Find the equation of a line from a gradient and a point.
Find the equation of a line through two points.
lessons.body:
The equation of a straight line is y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.

GRADIENT AND ONE POINT: y – y₁ = m(x – x₁).
Example 1. Gradient –1/3 through (–3, 2): y – 2 = –(1/3)(x + 3). Multiply by 3: 3y – 6 = –x – 3, so x + 3y = 3.

TWO POINTS: (y – y₁)/(y₂ – y₁) = (x – x₁)/(x₂ – x₁), or find m = (y₂ – y₁)/(x₂ – x₁) first and use the one-point form.
Example 2. Through (1, 4) and (–2, 6): m = (6 – 4)/(–2 – 1) = –2/3. y – 4 = –(2/3)(x – 1), so 3y – 12 = –2x + 2 and 2x + 3y = 14. Check (–2, 6): –4 + 18 = 14 ✓.

PARALLEL AND PERPENDICULAR. Example 3. The line through (2, 3) parallel to 4x – 2y = 1 (m = 2): y – 3 = 2(x – 2), y = 2x – 1. The line through (0, 4) perpendicular to y = –x/2 + 1 has m = 2: y = 2x + 4.

Intercepts: put y = 0 for the x-intercept and x = 0 for the y-intercept. For 3x – 4y = 12 these are (4, 0) and (0, –3).
